title: You can control *everything,* but *not the right time.*
description: Some projects arrive exactly when you expect them to. Others take their time. The rebranding of Salad Days belonged firmly in the second category.

blocks.heading: Some projects arrive exactly when you expect them to. Others take their time. The rebranding of Salad Days belonged firmly in the *second category.*

Long before there was a formal brief, there was a *friendship.* Over the course of more than <ref n="01"/> three years, countless conversations revolved around the brand, what it stood for, how people perceived it, and where it could go next. Every now and then those conversations turned into small collaborations, but the larger question of reimagining the brand always remained somewhere in the background.

annotations.text: The work started years before the timeline did.

blocks.heading: So when the opportunity finally arrived, it didn't feel like the beginning of a new project. It felt like the continuation<ref n="02"/> of a conversation that had been unfolding for years.

annotations.text: Meaningful creative work often begins long before a contract is signed, taking shape through conversations, observations, shared experiences, and accumulated understanding.

blocks.leftColumn: *One thing became clear almost immediately: this wasn't a brand that needed reinvention.*
blocks.rightColumn: Salad Days had already established a meaningful place in the lives of its customers. It had built recognition, familiarity, and a distinct personality over time. The challenge wasn't to create something entirely new, but to understand what people already connected with and strengthen those foundations for the future.

blocks.heading:
Like many rebranding projects, the process began by identifying the elements that carried the strongest memory value. Interestingly, one particular element kept resurfacing.

The *Teal.*

Whether we were reviewing past communication, discussing customer recall, or imagining future applications, the colour consistently found its way back into the conversation. It had become one of the brand's most recognizable assets—not because it was loud or distinctive in isolation, but because it had quietly earned its place over years of consistent use.

*The question was never whether it should remain. The question was whether it was the right teal.*

As the brand evolved, the existing colour no longer felt capable of carrying the growing ambitions of the business. We needed something with greater confidence and presence—something that could unify packaging, digital communication, retail environments, and future extensions of the brand without losing the familiarity people already associated with Salad Days.

The answer wasn't replacement. It was refinement.

While the teal remained at the center of the identity, the broader colour system required a more significant evolution.

Consumer brands live across an enormous range of touchpoints. Menus, packaging, social media, campaigns, merchandise, seasonal launches, and promotional materials all compete for attention. Relying too heavily on a single colour can eventually create repetition rather than recognition.

The challenge was to build a system that felt cohesive without becoming predictable.

By introducing a complementary palette, we created a framework that allowed the brand to communicate with greater flexibility while maintaining a consistent visual voice. The objective wasn't variety for the sake of variety. It was creating a system capable of growing alongside the brand.
